## Executive summary

The price of college has risen far faster than inflation. Real published tuition per credit at American colleges rose 55% between 2002 and 2024, and 73% at public four-year universities. States responded with three decades of policy aimed at getting students to a degree faster and more cheaply: transferable general-education cores and guaranteed transfer of associate degrees, dual-enrollment programs that let high-school students earn college credit, mandates that public universities accept AP scores, excess-credit surcharges, and guided pathways that map the shortest route to a degree. Most of these work by moving the production of credit away from the expensive university to a cheaper community college, a high-school classroom or an exam. Did they work? No national dataset follows a student's credits from where they were earned to the degree they count toward, so the question has been hard to answer.

This paper uses a simple measure that can see the result, if not its causes. The **efficiency ratio** (ER) divides the credits embodied in the degrees an institution awards (120 for a bachelor's, 60 for an associate degree) by the undergraduate credits it teaches in the same year. Students who drop out, change majors or take more courses than they need push the ratio below 1. Students who arrive with credits earned somewhere else, through AP, dual enrollment or transfer, push it up, and can push it above 1. Summed across all colleges, credit moved from one college to another cancels out, so the national ratio rises only if the system as a whole teaches fewer credits per degree.

The ratio barely moved for more than a decade, then rose sharply. American colleges awarded about 58 credits' worth of degrees for every 100 credits they taught from 1998 to 2011, and 80 by 2022. The rise was large, broad and concentrated in public institutions. Public four-year universities went from 0.68 in 2010 to 0.90 in 2022, and public research universities reached 1.0; community colleges doubled, from 0.23 to 0.45. Private nonprofit colleges gained only 9%, and private R1 universities did not move. Every state's public system rose. The share of public four-year institutions that certify more degree credit than they teach tripled, to 30%.

The easy explanations account for little of it. Shrinking entering classes after the recession surge raised the ratio mechanically, but at elasticities estimated across institutions within Carnegie classes, they explain 5% of the public four-year rise and 8% of the nonprofit rise. Completion explains more, in a telling way: at public universities, four-year completion rose from 31% to 45% between 2010 and 2022 while six-year completion rose only from 56% to 63%, which is what one would see if more students arrived with credits in hand. Fewer students leaving without a degree adds the same small amount at public and nonprofit universities and explains none of the gap between them. Meanwhile, colleges teach their enrolled students, on average, the same 23 to 25 credits a year they always have. What fell is teaching per degree: by half at community colleges, by a quarter at public universities, and by 8% at nonprofits.

For public universities, the evidence leans toward what I call **credit outsourcing**: a growing share of each bachelor's degree is produced somewhere other than the university that awards it. About 42% of public bachelor's degrees go to students who transferred in. In 2023–24, 2.8 million high-school students took college courses for credit, and 3.8 million AP exams earned qualifying scores in 2024. The five largest online universities, which accept up to 90 transferred, tested or prior-learning credits, saw their combined ratio rise from 0.59 to 0.96.

For the nation, the picture is more favorable. Ballpark accounting attributes 3–5% of the national rise to cohort timing, 4–9% to fewer students leaving, at most 5–10% to AP credit and at most a fifth to associate degrees counted on the way to a bachelor's. The large residual, about 70% at the midpoints, most plausibly reflects students who finish taking fewer failed, repeated and abandoned courses, through reform or through easier grading. State-by-state accounting gives the same split.

The ratio absorbed most of the price increase. Published tuition per degree rose only 18% between 2002 and 2024; net tuition revenue per degree did not rise; and the net cost of attendance per degree, counting living costs and grants, fell 8%. Part of that saving is real. Part is cost moved to cheaper providers, where grant aid now covers the full tuition of the average first-time, full-time community-college student. And part raises a question no institutional dataset can answer: whether a degree assembled from AP, dual-enrollment and community-college credit is the same product as one taught in full by the university whose name it bears.

## 1. Introduction

Most people picture the path to a college degree this way: a student finishes high school, enrolls at one university, earns the 120 credits a bachelor's degree requires over four years, and graduates. That was my story and the story of most people I knew in college. It describes fewer and fewer students. AP exams have tripled in twenty years. Dual-enrollment courses, taken for college credit while still in high school, now enroll nearly three million students a year. Transfer between institutions, once a detour, is a main road: two of every five bachelor's degrees at public universities go to students who started somewhere else.

Much of this was deliberate. Since the 1990s, states have built transferable general-education cores, guaranteed that associate degrees transfer with junior standing, funded high-school students to take college courses, and required public universities to award credit for AP scores. The aim was to make degrees faster and cheaper by moving part of their production to lower-cost providers. There has been remarkably little evidence on whether that happened at scale, mainly because no national dataset follows individual students' credits from where they were earned to the degree they count toward.

Public policy was not the only force. The for-profit sector built credit earned elsewhere into its model long before states did. The University of Phoenix, founded in 1976, enrolled working adults who brought much of their first two years with them as transfer and prior-learning credit ([Phoenix](https://www.phoenix.edu/blog/what-are-prior-learning-assessments.html)). The sector peaked at just over 2.0 million students in fall 2010 and then lost more than half of them in a decade of closures and regulation: Corinthian in 2015, ITT in 2016, the Education Management and Dream Center collapse in 2018–19 ([NCES Digest 303.10](https://nces.ed.gov/programs/digest/d22/tables/dt22_303.10.asp)). What was new around 2010 was not credit for experience, which predates the closures, but a third-party "alternative credit" industry that grew alongside the decline: low-cost online courses carrying American Council on Education credit recommendations, from StraighterLine (founded 2009) to ACE's Alternative Credit Project (2014).

The large online universities that grew in the same years accept that credit at scale. Western Governors (competency-based since 1999), Southern New Hampshire, Liberty, Grand Canyon and Phoenix each accept roughly 90 transfer, exam or prior-learning credits toward a 120-credit bachelor's degree. In 2013 SNHU's College for America became the first program approved for federal aid on direct assessment of competencies rather than credit hours ([New America](https://newamerica.org/higher-education/higher-ed-watch/its-official-us-department-of-education-approves-first-college-to-ditch-the-credit-hour)). Only Phoenix has been for-profit throughout: Western Governors, SNHU and Liberty are nonprofits, and Grand Canyon converted to nonprofit status in 2018, a status the Department of Education still contests. In 2024 these five taught about 3% of undergraduate credits but awarded 4.4% of bachelor's degrees, and their combined efficiency ratio rose from 0.59 in 2010 to 0.96 in 2022 (Table 2).

This paper takes an indirect route to the question of where degree credit is produced. Every college reports to the federal government, each year, how many undergraduate credits it taught and how many degrees it awarded. Dividing one by the other gives a production ratio, which I call the efficiency ratio: degree credits awarded per credit taught. If degrees increasingly rest on credits produced elsewhere, the ratio rises at the institutions that import them. If students waste fewer credits on the way to a degree, it rises too. The ratio cannot by itself separate those stories, but the patterns in it, across sectors, states, types of institution and time, can.

The paper asks four questions. How has the ratio behaved since 1998, and where did it move? How much of its movement reflects measurable fundamentals: the size of entering classes, retention and completion? What does a rising ratio imply for what students pay per degree? And is the rise better described as institutions producing degrees more efficiently, or as institutions outsourcing part of their curriculum to other providers?

Section 2 reviews the policies that set out to change where credits are earned. Section 3 defines the efficiency ratio. Section 4 documents its path and how much of it cohort timing explains. Section 5 turns to cost. Section 6 examines the channels through which outside credit arrives: dual enrollment, AP and transfer-oriented certificates. Section 7 weighs outsourcing against efficiency using direct evidence on completion, teaching per degree and who earns degrees. Section 8 closes with a ballpark accounting of the national and state rise, which draws on everything before it. Section 9 concludes.

*Each figure has an interactive counterpart on the companion page "Credits In, Degrees Out." Links to specific views will be added when the page moves to its permanent site.*

## 2. The policy push

### 2.1 The problem states set out to solve

Two concerns drove three decades of state policy. The first was time and credits to degree. Students routinely took far more than 120 credits and five or six years to finish a bachelor's degree, and every extra semester cost students, families and taxpayers. The second was credit lost in transfer. Students moving between institutions frequently found that courses they had passed counted only as electives, or not at all. The Government Accountability Office estimated that students who transferred between 2004 and 2009 lost about 43% of their credits, and 37% even when moving between public institutions ([GAO-17-574](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-17-574)).

After 2008 those concerns merged into a national completion agenda. The Lumina Foundation set a goal of 60% of working-age adults holding a credential by 2025. Complete College America, founded in 2009, pushed states toward structured degree maps, full-time course loads and "15 to Finish" campaigns. In 2012 six foundations launched Credit When It's Due, which funded reverse-transfer programs in 12 states and later 15. The federal government stayed largely on the sidelines; the binding action was in state legislatures and system offices.

### 2.2 The levers

States pulled a handful of levers, summarized in Table 1 with the year each state adopted them where a source gives one. They differ in mechanism, but with two exceptions, guided pathways and excess-credit surcharges, they share a common feature: they move the production of credit away from the institution that awards the degree.

Only the first two rows act on how efficiently an institution teaches its own students. Everything below them works by relocating credit production: to another college, to a high-school classroom, or to an exam. A rising efficiency ratio is therefore precisely what most of these policies were designed to produce, whether or not they made higher education cheaper in total.

The dates show recognizable waves. Dual enrollment and the first general-education cores came in the 1980s and early 1990s. Transfer cores, common course numbering and guaranteed associate-degree transfer spread through the 1990s. The completion agenda arrived in 2008–2009, and a second, denser wave followed in 2010–2015: California's Associate Degree for Transfer and Tennessee's transfer pathways in 2010, reverse-transfer statutes in 2011–2013, guided pathways and "15 to Finish" from 2011, and most AP mandates after 2015. The national efficiency ratio turned up in 2011, at the start of the second wave (Section 4); timing alone does not show that the policies caused the rise.

### 2.3 What the evidence shows

The research base is thinner than the policy activity. Statewide articulation policies were designed to prevent credit loss rather than to raise transfer, and the best-known study of them, Roksa and Keith (2008), found no higher transfer rates in states that had them. Transfer students in those states had slightly higher bachelor's completion, 61% against 57%, but slightly longer time to degree. Gross and Goldhaber (2009) and LaSota and Zumeta (2016) likewise found limited effects of statewide transfer policies. Excess credit-hour surcharges fare worse. In a 2000–2013 panel of institutions, Kramer, Holcomb and Kelchen found no detectable effect on four- or six-year graduation rates, but median student debt rose 5.7–7.2% four years after adoption, more for low-income students ([AERA](https://www.aera.net/Newsroom/News-Releases-and-Statements/State-Adopted-Credit-Hour-Policies-Associated-with-Increases-in-Student-Debt-but-Not-Graduation-Rates)).

Dual enrollment has the strongest evidence. The What Works Clearinghouse rates it as having positive effects on college degree attainment, college enrollment and credit accumulation ([WWC, 2017](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/interventionreport/671)). Following more than 200,000 students who took community-college courses in high school in fall 2010, the Community College Research Center found that 88% continued in college after high school, with wide gaps by state and income ([Fink, Jenkins and Yanagiura, 2017](https://ccrc.tc.columbia.edu/publications/what-happens-community-college-dual-enrollment-students.html)). AP credit mandates have barely been studied. Credit for prior learning has some evidence: in a 2020 study of 230,000 adult students at 72 institutions, those with prior-learning credit completed at higher rates, but only 11% of adults used it ([CAEL and WICHE](https://www.cael.org/hubfs/PLA%20Boost%20Fact%20Sheet%20CAEL%20WICHE%20-%20Oct%202020.pdf)). Reverse transfer works mechanically: Credit When It's Due states conferred about 15,860 associate degrees between 2012 and 2016, degrees that required no additional teaching.

### 2.4 Why the evidence is scarce

The outcome these policies target lives in transcripts. Whether a policy changed how many credits a graduate brought in, how many were lost, or how many were taken in total can be seen only in course-level records. National transcript studies are periodic, small and restricted, and state longitudinal systems lose students who cross state lines or attend private institutions. Institutional data record the wrong flows: the federal survey reports credits taught and degrees awarded, not credits imported per graduate, and the National Student Clearinghouse records enrollment and degrees but not credits. The policies were also bundled: transfer guarantees, reverse transfer, guided pathways and performance funding arrived in the same states in the same years. And measured gains can be mechanical: a policy that imports credit raises on-time graduation without any change in instruction, which in the absence of transcripts looks like efficiency.

I do not estimate policy effects in this paper. What I offer instead is a system-level indicator that moves when an institution's degrees rest on credit produced elsewhere, and evidence that it moved a great deal after 2010.

## 3. Measuring degree production

### 3.1 The efficiency ratio

The efficiency ratio asks a simple question of each institution in each year: for every undergraduate credit it teaches, how many credits' worth of degrees does it award? Counting a bachelor's degree as 120 semester credits and an associate degree as 60,

```latex
ER_{it} = \frac{120 \cdot \text{bachelor's}_{it} + 60 \cdot \text{associate}_{it}}{\text{undergraduate semester credit hours taught}_{it}}
```

Aggregates for a sector, a state or the nation add up degree credits and credits taught across institutions, so they are weighted averages of institution ratios, with each institution weighted by the credits it teaches.

The ratio is a production measure. It counts output, degree credits certified, per unit of the main input an institution controls, instruction delivered. Consider a college where every entering student finishes in exactly the credits the degree requires, all of them taken there, and where enrollment is steady. Its ER would be exactly 1. That benchmark is the same for a community college as for a university, because an associate degree is counted at its own 60 credits. Real institutions fall short of it for familiar reasons, and a growing number exceed it for reasons that are the subject of this paper.

### 3.2 What pushes the ratio down

Three things hold the ratio below 1. The largest is students who do not finish: credits taught to a student who drops out or transfers out before earning a degree enter the denominator with nothing in the numerator. Low completion is the main reason community colleges sat near 0.23 until 2010. The second is students who finish but take more than they need, because they changed majors, repeated courses that they failed or withdrew from, or took electives beyond the requirement. The third is instruction that never aims at a degree: courses taken by non-degree students, by certificate seekers (certificates are not counted in the headline ratio), and by high-school students in dual enrollment.

### 3.3 What moves it over time

Some forces that move the ratio over time can be measured directly. The most mechanical is the size of entering classes. Credits are taught to every enrolled class, but degrees go to classes that entered four to six years earlier. When entering classes grow, credits rise before degrees do and the ratio falls; when they shrink, it rises, even if nothing about the efficiency of instruction has changed. For four-year institutions I measure growth as the two newest entering classes relative to the classes that entered four and five years earlier. Retention matters for a similar reason: more first-year students returning means more credits taught now and, if they finish, more degrees later. And completion matters most of all, since a higher share of entrants finishing, and finishing faster, raises degrees per credit taught.

Two other forces cannot be measured in institutional data, and they are the ones this paper is about. The first is **imported credit**. A student who arrives with 30 credits from AP exams, dual enrollment or a community college needs only 90 more from the university. The degree still counts as 120 credits in the university's numerator, but only 90 appear in its denominator. Imported credit can push an institution's ratio above 1, and it is the main reason an institution would stay there for long. The second is **genuine efficiency** inside the institution: better advising, clearer degree maps, fewer dead-end courses, fewer failures. Both raise the ratio. Neither is recorded in the federal data, because institutions report what they teach and what they award, not how many credits each graduate brought with them.

### 3.4 Outsourcing, and why the nation is different

Imported credit is also a measure of how much of a university's degree has been produced somewhere else. When a public university's ratio rises from 0.68 to 0.90 while the credits it teaches each student stay flat, part of each bachelor's degree it awards may be produced by community colleges, by high schools offering dual credit, and by the AP program. I call that **credit outsourcing**. It is not necessarily bad. Those providers are usually cheaper, and states pursued exactly this outcome on purpose. But it changes what a degree from a given university contains, who pays for which part of it, and how that university's spending per degree should be read.

Outsourcing has a limit that matters for interpreting the national numbers. It raises the ratio of the institution that imports credit, but it cannot by itself raise the ratio for the nation as a whole. A credit taught at a community college and later counted toward a bachelor's degree is still in some institution's denominator; summed over all colleges, it appears once. The national ratio rises only when degree credit rests on credit taught nowhere in the system (AP, and also CLEP, IB, military and prior-learning credit); when the same taught credits count toward two degrees, as when a student earns an associate degree and then a bachelor's; when fewer credits go to students who never finish; when students who do finish take fewer excess credits; or when cohort timing shifts. The institution story and the national story are therefore different questions. Sections 6 and 7 take up the first; Section 8 the second.

### 3.5 Data

The analysis uses an institution-by-year panel of all U.S. 2- and 4-year institutions built from the federal Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), 1998–2024. Credit hours are each institution's 12-month undergraduate credit-hour activity, converted to semester units for quarter-calendar schools. Before 2002 the same item comes from older surveys, which I splice on with care; those years are shaded in the figures. Degrees are first-major bachelor's and associate degrees. A set of screens, applied identically in every year, removes non-reporting years, implausible values and unit errors, such as a few institutions that reported courses rather than credits for some years. Appendix A gives the details. A stable panel of about 2,500 institutions present in nearly every year follows the same national path as the full sample, so the patterns below are not an artifact of institutions entering or leaving the data. The 2024 data are provisional.

## 4. Two decades of the efficiency ratio

### 4.1 A long plateau, then a decade of increases

Figure 1 shows the national efficiency ratio from 1998 to 2024. For more than a decade nothing happened. The ratio was 0.59 in 1998 and 0.56 in 2010, wobbling with the business cycle but showing no trend. Then it rose every year from 2011 to 2022, reaching 0.80, before falling back to 0.75 by 2024.

![Figure 1](figures/WP3_01_national_er.png)

**Figure 1. The national efficiency ratio, 1998–2024.** Credit-hour-weighted aggregate of all in-sample 2- and 4-year institutions, with the median institution and the 10th–90th percentile range across degree-granting institutions. Repository table T1.

The rise was not driven by a few outliers or by credit hours shifting toward institutions that were already efficient. The whole distribution moved. Between 2010 and 2022 the median institution went from 0.53 to 0.73, the 10th percentile from 0.16 to 0.30, and the 90th percentile from 0.99 to 1.16. Within four-year institutions alone the median went from 0.72 to 0.89, and within two-year institutions from 0.24 to 0.42. Typical institutions changed.

### 4.2 A public-sector story

Figure 2 breaks the aggregate down by control and level, and Table 2 gives the levels at four benchmark years. The rise belongs to public institutions. Public four-year universities, flat at 0.68 through 2010, reached 0.90 by 2022, a rise of 32%. Public two-year colleges doubled, from 0.23 to 0.45. Private nonprofit four-year colleges, which started near 0.83, gained 9%. For-profit four-year institutions rose 66% on a rapidly shrinking base; the rise holds among the 152 institutions present in both years, from 0.48 to 0.83. The five largest online universities, which span the nonprofit and for-profit sectors, rose from 0.59 to 0.96. Every sector fell after 2022.

The contrast is sharpest among research universities (Figure 3). Every public class rose, and the gaps among public research, doctoral and master's universities closed: by 2022 all sat near 1.0. Public R1 universities rose from 0.88 in 2010 to 0.99 in 2022. Public baccalaureate colleges and the community colleges that now award a few bachelor's degrees rose most, by 60% and 116%. Private nonprofit R1 universities, by contrast, sat at about 0.90 for the entire period, and no private nonprofit class other than the small Associate group rose by more than 11%. One plausible difference is how many students arrive through state transfer pipelines and with state-guaranteed credit. I do not measure transfer intake by Carnegie class, so the contrast is suggestive rather than conclusive, but it is the first of several patterns that fit imported credit better than internal efficiency.

### 4.3 Every state

The rise was national. Figure 4 plots each state's public system, its public two- and four-year institutions pooled, in 2010 and 2022. Every one of the 51 public systems rose. The largest gains came in states with big community-college systems and active transfer policy: California rose 0.36, Arkansas 0.34, Oregon, New Mexico and Maryland 0.33. The smallest came in small northeastern and mountain systems, New Hampshire and Vermont (0.11), Maine (0.13) and Montana (0.14). By 2024 the public four-year systems of Maryland, Kansas and Connecticut were at or near 1.

![Figure 4](figures/WP3_04_states_2010_2022.png)

**Figure 4. Efficiency ratio of each state's public system, 2010 and 2022.** Public 2- and 4-year institutions pooled within each state. Repository table T18a. Interactive version: the state map, with a year slider.

### 4.4 Institutions that award more than they teach

An institution whose ratio exceeds 1 certifies more degree credit than it teaches, which over any sustained period most plausibly reflects imported credit. Figure 5 tracks how common that has become among four-year institutions. In 2010, 9% of public four-year institutions had a ratio above 1, against 19% of private nonprofits. By 2022 the public share had more than tripled, to 30%, matching the private nonprofit share. Across all institutions, the number above 1 went from 377 in 2010 to 736 in 2022, before falling to 546 in 2024. Most of those that crossed 1 did not go far past it: the public share above 1.2 only doubled, from 4% to 9%. The movement is a broad shift of the distribution, not a few institutions running off the scale.

![Figure 5](figures/WP3_05_share_above_threshold.png)

**Figure 5. Share of 4-year institutions with ER above 1, by control.** Repository table T20. Interactive version: threshold slider from 0.50 to 1.20.

Community colleges are measured against the same benchmark, since an associate degree counts at its own 60 credits, and they fall far short of it. In 2022 public two-year colleges taught 132 credits for every degree they awarded, more than twice the 60 an associate degree requires, and their ratio was 0.45. Only 20 of 1,096 two-year colleges, 2%, had a ratio above 1. That is down from 267 credits per degree in 2010, but most community-college teaching still does not end in that college's credential. It goes to students who transfer before finishing, to certificates, to high-school students in dual enrollment and to students who leave. Section 6.4 returns to what that means for the four-year side of the ledger.

### 4.5 How much is cohort timing?

The first worry about any ratio of a flow to a stock is timing. Credits go to every enrolled class, but degrees go to classes that entered years earlier. The years around 2010 are exactly the pattern that would mislead: a recession surge in entering classes followed by a decade of shrinking ones. Public four-year entering-class growth peaked at 1.15 in 2010 and fell to 0.95 by 2022; at private nonprofits the swing was smaller, from 1.03 to 0.97 (Figure 6, left). At community colleges it was far larger. First-time entrants at public two-year colleges rose from 790,000 to 1.0 million between the classes entering in fall 2007 and fall 2009, so growth reached 1.30 in 2011 and fell to 0.81 by 2022. That spike is real, not a reporting artifact.

I estimate the size of the timing effect from institutions, not from state or national aggregates, which load anything else that moved with the national cohort cycle onto growth. Table 3 regresses each four-year institution's log ER on the log of its own entering-class growth, 1998–2024, separately for public and private nonprofit institutions, with year fixed effects throughout and with and without fixed effects for the institution's Carnegie research class. For-profit institutions are left out: their enrollment swung enormously and for reasons unrelated to the timing of degrees, and in pooled regressions they dominate the estimate (Appendix Table B4).

The Carnegie controls matter, and for a telling reason. Across public Carnegie classes, growth and the ratio move together: R1 universities have the highest ratios (0.89) and grew fastest, while the community colleges classified as four-year have the lowest (0.31) and barely grew. Within a class, faster growth goes with a lower ratio, as timing predicts. Without the controls the public coefficient is slightly positive; with them it is −0.076. At nonprofits the controls move the estimate from −0.085 to −0.128. I use columns 2 and 4: a 10% larger pair of entering classes lowers a public university's ratio by about 0.7% and a nonprofit's by about 1.2%.

Those are small effects, smaller than the timing arithmetic alone would suggest. If every class grew at the same rate and nothing else differed, degrees would lag credits by about three years and the elasticity would be about −0.75. Institution-level growth is noisy, which pulls estimates toward zero, but the gap is large. Figure 6 shows both.

![Figure 6](figures/WP3_06_cohort_growth.png)

**Figure 6. Entering-class growth and the ER net of growth, public and private nonprofit 4-year institutions.** Net series hold growth at its 1998 level, using the elasticities of Table 3 (dashed) and the mechanical value of −0.75 (dotted). Repository table T24.

At the estimated elasticities, cohort timing explains 5% of the public four-year rise between 2010 and 2022 (0.011 of 0.218 ER points) and 8% of the nonprofit rise (0.006 of 0.075). For the two sectors combined it explains 6% of the rise and 8% of the decline after 2022. Net of growth, the public ratio still climbs from 0.69 to 0.90. Even the mechanical bound, which no regression supports, explains only about half of the 2010–2022 rise in either sector, and its net public series still rises from 0.73 to 0.84. I do not estimate an elasticity for two-year colleges; their much larger swing in entering classes means timing could matter more there (Section 6.4). First-year retention, the other mechanical candidate, explains almost nothing: about 0.01 ER points or less.

The conclusion of this section is that the rise is large, recent, broad across institutions and states, and concentrated in the public sector, and that cohort timing explains only a small part of it.

## 5. What a higher ratio means for the cost of a degree

### 5.1 Price per credit and price per degree

A rising efficiency ratio changes the arithmetic of college prices. If students pay a price p per credit and an institution awards degrees at ratio ER, the tuition it collects per bachelor's-equivalent degree is

```latex
\text{tuition per degree} = \frac{p \times 120}{ER}
```

so the index of tuition per degree is the price index divided by the ER index. When the ratio rises, each degree brings the institution less tuition than the per-credit price suggests. I measure price three ways, all in real 2024 dollars: published tuition and fees (in-district for community colleges, in-state for other public institutions); undergraduate net tuition revenue after discounts and allowances, from institutional finance reports beginning in 2003; and the net cost of attendance, the federal net price for first-time full-time aid recipients beginning in 2009. Net cost of attendance covers tuition, fees, housing, food, books and transportation, net of grants. It belongs in a per-credit calculation for a simple reason: in any year a student pays for the credits they take, but also for everything else that comes with the year in which they take them. A credit stands for its share of that whole bundle. Using it per degree assumes that institutions aid transfer students much as they aid first-time, full-time students. Every aggregate is a credit-hour-weighted average of institutions' own prices, divided by the same institutions' aggregate ratio.

### 5.2 Nation and sectors

The rising ratio absorbed most of the increase in prices (Figure 7, Table 4). Real published tuition per credit rose 55% between 2002 and 2024. Tuition per degree rose 18%; net tuition revenue per degree did not rise at all, and the net cost of attendance per degree fell 8%. Had the national ratio stayed at its 2010 level, tuition per degree in 2024 would have been about a third higher. The timing follows the ratio: while the ratio was flat, per-credit and per-degree prices moved together, so tuition per degree peaked in 2010 and has fallen since.

![Figure 7](figures/WP3_07_tuition_per_degree.png)

**Figure 7. Real prices per credit and per degree, nation and sectors, 2002–2024.** Index, 2002 = 100. Repository table T18. Interactive version: the tuition section, with measure and view selectors.

**Table 4. Real price indexes in 2024 (2002 = 100)**

|  | Published tuition per credit | ER | Published tuition per degree | Net tuition revenue per degree | Net cost of attendance per degree |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All 2- and 4-year | 155 | 131 | 118 | 99 | 92 |
| Public 4-year | 173 | 124 | 139 | 126 | 114 |
| Community colleges | 149 | 190 | 78 | 57 | 60 |
| Private nonprofit 4-year | 137 | 105 | 131 | 98 | 106 |
| Private for-profit 4-year | 90 | 147 | 62 | 56 | 59 |

*Net tuition revenue is linked to the published-tuition index in 2003 and net cost of attendance in 2009, so they measure growth from those years on a 2002 base. Source: author's calculations from IPEDS charges, finance and student aid files; CPI-U. Repository table T18.*

The sectors tell different stories. At public four-year universities, real tuition rose 73% while tuition per degree rose 39%; in dollars, tuition per bachelor's-equivalent went from about $33,500 to $46,600, and net tuition revenue per degree lands at the same figure, a useful check that the published-price measure is not far off. The net cost of attendance per degree rose only 14%. At community colleges, in-district tuition rose 49%, but because the ratio nearly doubled, tuition per degree fell 22%, and on net revenue and net cost it fell 40% or more. At private nonprofits the published-price and revenue measures diverge: tuition per degree rose 31% on sticker prices but was flat on net revenue, a reminder that rising discounts make sticker prices misleading in that sector.

### 5.3 States

The state view pools each state's public two- and four-year institutions, each at its own price (Figure 8). Within that pool, a credit taught at a community college and later counted toward a bachelor's at the state university stays inside the system, so this measure comes closer to what a public system collects per degree it produces. In the median state, real published tuition per credit rose 72% while tuition per degree rose 25%. The ratio did the most work in California, where real public tuition per credit rose 160% but tuition per degree only 54%; large gains in the ratio also offset large tuition increases in Nevada, Oregon, Texas and Georgia. Only Maryland, Florida and New Mexico collect less published tuition per degree than in 2002. Where tuition per degree rose most, in Arizona, Virginia and Colorado, tuition increases simply outran gains in the ratio.

The other two price measures tell the same story at lower levels. On net tuition revenue, the median state's price per credit rose 51% and its price per degree 12%, and 15 of 51 systems collect less per degree than in 2002. On net cost of attendance, the median state's price per degree rose only 2%, and 23 systems are below their 2002 level, led by New Mexico (−56%), Florida and Nevada. Figures 8b and 8c show those versions; one of the three will appear in the final paper, and the others on the interactive page.
