### 5.4 Saving or shifting?

The state measure already captures one kind of shifting. Each credit is priced at the institution that teaches it, so when a state moves lower-division credit from its universities to its community colleges, the system's price per degree falls in Figure 8 by exactly the price gap between them. And because net cost of attendance counts grants, Figure 8c also captures "free" community college: since 2009–10, grant aid has on average covered the full tuition of first-time full-time public two-year students ([College Board](https://research.collegeboard.org/trends/college-pricing/highlights)). In 2024–25 average published tuition and fees were $4,050 at public two-year colleges and $11,610 at public four-year institutions ([College Board, via NASFAA](https://www.nasfaa.org/news-item/34985/Sticker_v_Net_Price_in_2024-25_The_College_Board_Breaks_Down_What_Students_Actually_Pay_to_Attend_College)), and community-college students more often live at home.

What the state measure cannot say is whether the system also teaches fewer credits per degree. A lower price per degree can come from teaching the same credits at cheaper places, or from teaching fewer of them. The first is a shift of where the money is spent, with taxpayers carrying part of the cost through appropriations to community colleges and dual-enrollment programs; the second is a saving. Section 8's accounting addresses that split. Three pieces sit outside the state measure altogether: AP credit, which costs the student a $99 exam and the system nothing; dual-enrollment credit taught in high schools, which is counted at the college's published price but is often waived or discounted; and credit carried across state lines. A full accounting of public cost per degree, including state appropriations and federal aid, is beyond this paper.

## 6. The channels

Three channels bring credit into a university from outside: dual enrollment, AP and transfer from community colleges, increasingly packaged as certificates built for that purpose. Dual enrollment, AP and transfer-oriented certificates grew while the ratio rose; transfer volume did not (Section 7.5). None can yet be traced into individual degrees, but their size and timing are informative, and they frame the tests in Section 7.

### 6.1 Dual enrollment

In 2022–23 IPEDS began counting, for the first time, the high-school students who take college courses for credit during the year. The numbers are large and growing. Dual enrollment reached 2.51 million students in 2022–23 and 2.82 million in 2023–24, a 13% increase in a single year (Table 5). At public two-year colleges, dual-enrollment students are 23% of everyone enrolled during the year; at the median such college they are a quarter. About 95% of public two-year colleges enroll them, and 103 institutions are majority high-school students. In Indiana they are half of public two-year enrollment, Ivy Tech alone counting 91,000; in Iowa and North Dakota they exceed 40%. California, Texas and New York have the most in absolute terms, at 292,000, 284,000 and 176,000.

**Table 5. Dual enrollment by sector, 2023–24**

| Sector | Dual-enrolled students | Share of 12-month undergraduates | Institutions with 25%+ | Institutions with 50%+ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Public 2-year | 1,413,000 | 22.7% | 409 | 57 |
| Public 4-year | 1,158,000 | 11.3% | 147 | 21 |
| Private nonprofit 4-year | 243,000 | 6.7% | 89 | 23 |
| All institutions | 2,824,000 | 12.9% | 663 | 103 |

*Source: author's calculations from IPEDS 12-Month Enrollment, high-school student counts. Repository table T8. Several large community-college districts that award a few bachelor's degrees are coded public 4-year, which raises that sector's count.*

The direct count exists for only two years, so to see the trend I use fall enrollment of undergraduates under 18, which IPEDS has collected in odd years since the 1980s. A fall snapshot misses students enrolled only in spring or summer: in 2023–24 the full-year count at public two-year colleges was 1.53 times the fall under-18 count at the same institutions, a ratio that barely moved between the two overlap years (1.57 in 2022–23) and is consistent with the Community College Research Center's finding that fall counts capture about 60% of the full-year total. Applying that ratio to earlier falls implies about 130,000 full-year dual enrollees at public two-year colleges in 1987, 580,000 in 2009, and 1.1 million in 2019, against the direct count of 1.4 million in 2023–24 (Figure 9). Most of the growth came after 2011, in step with the rise in the efficiency ratio.

![Figure 9](figures/WP3_09_dual_enrollment.png)

**Figure 9. Estimated full-year dual enrollment at public 2-year colleges, 1987–2023.** Fall under-18 undergraduates scaled by the 2023–24 full-year ratio. Repository tables T9–T10a.

At an assumed 6–9 credits per student per year (IPEDS does not report it), 2.8 million dual enrollees take 17–25 million credits, 4–7% of all undergraduate credits taught. Those credits sit in the teaching college's denominator, where they hold its ratio down. When a student later carries them to a university, they raise that university's degree credits without adding to its credits taught.

### 6.2 Advanced Placement

AP credit never enters IPEDS: no college teaches it, and no survey asks how much a graduate brought. The College Board's exam counts are the best measure of supply. The number of AP exams scoring 3 or higher rose from 1.16 million in 2004 to 1.86 million in 2010, 2.87 million in 2022 and 3.83 million in 2024, the last jump reflecting a change in scoring practice (Figure 10). By student, 22.6% of the public high-school class of 2024, some 786,000 graduates, scored 3 or higher on at least one exam ([College Board](https://reports.collegeboard.org/ap-program-results/class-of-2024)). More than 2,100 institutions award credit for AP scores, and 37 states require public institutions to award credit for a 3 (Table 1).

![Figure 10](figures/WP3_10_ap_exams.png)

**Figure 10. AP exams scoring 3 or higher and the national ER, 2004–2024.** Index, 2004 = 100. Sources: College Board AP Score Distributions; repository table T1.

At the point of entry AP looms large. The 3.8 million qualifying exams of 2024 compare with about 1.26 million first-time freshmen at four-year institutions. If each replaced one course of a ten-course first year, AP would displace up to 30% of first-year courses at four-year institutions; the true share is lower, because many qualifying exams are taken by students who go to two-year colleges or do not enroll, and some earn no credit. Relative to all instruction, however, AP is small: at three credits per qualifying exam, it amounts to about 3% of undergraduate credits taught. And its timing does not match the ratio's. Qualifying exams grew 60% between 2004 and 2010, while the ratio did not move. AP matters a great deal to some universities, but it is not the main story nationally (Section 8).

### 6.3 Certificates built for transfer

Community-college certificates tripled between 2002 and 2025, from 258,000 to 779,000, rising from 0.59 to 0.92 certificates per associate degree. Most of the growth is short vocational awards in business, information technology, welding and mechanics. But the single largest source of growth since 2010 is something else: general-education certificates (CIP 24.01), which rose from 16,000 to 125,000 and account for 30% of all net certificate growth (Figure 11). Unlike vocational certificates, 78% of these are awards of one year or longer, and 51% are awarded in California, where they are mostly CSU GE-Breadth and IGETC certificates of achievement. They certify a completed block of lower-division general education that will be counted toward a bachelor's degree somewhere else: the same channel the efficiency ratio detects at the receiving end. Counting them as output at the community college and again inside the bachelor's degree they feed would count the same credit twice.

![Figure 11](figures/WP3_11_cc_certificates.png)

**Figure 11. Community-college certificates by field group, 2010 and 2025.** Ten field groups with the largest growth. Repository table T11b.

### 6.4 The community-college side of the ledger

Community colleges' own ratio doubled, and it doubled in an unusual way (Figure 12). From 1998 to 2010 it sat at about 0.23, with associate degrees and credits taught growing in step; the fixed group of community colleges in Figure 12 taught about 260 credits per associate degree. Between 2010 and 2022 associate degrees rose 41% while credits taught fell 29%, as fall headcount dropped by a quarter, and credits taught per degree halved, to 130. Part of this is the enrollment cycle: the recession surge in entering classes, 1.30 times the classes four and five years earlier at its 2011 peak, filled classrooms before it produced degrees, and its unwinding did the reverse. A shorter window suited to two-year programs, (Eₜ + Eₜ₋₁) ÷ (Eₜ₋₂ + Eₜ₋₃), shows the same swing, from 1.22 in 2010 to 0.82 in 2022. I do not estimate a timing elasticity for two-year colleges. Part is reform: the Associate Degree for Transfer and guided pathways aim at exactly this, more students finishing a credential before they move on. Reverse transfer adds associate degrees with no new teaching at all.

![Figure 12](figures/WP3_12_community_colleges.png)

**Figure 12. Community colleges: associate degrees, credits taught and the ER, 1998–2024.** Index, 2002 = 100. Repository table T17.

Dual enrollment holds the community colleges' measured ratio down, because credits taught to high-school students rarely become a community-college degree. Removing an estimated 6–9 credits per dual enrollee raises the 2022 ratio of the community colleges in Figure 12 from 0.47 to 0.52–0.55. (That fixed group sits slightly above the public two-year sector as a whole, at 0.45 in Table 2.) And most community-college credits still do not end in that college's degree. They go to students who transfer before finishing, to certificates, to dual enrollment and to students who leave. The credits that transfer and count toward a bachelor's appear as output at the receiving university: they are the other half of the four-year outsourcing story.

## 7. Outsourcing or efficiency?

An institution's ratio can rise because it imports more credit or because it wastes less. This section sets out what each explanation predicts (Table 6), tests the measurable fundamentals directly, and asks where the fall in teaching per degree happened.

### 7.1 What each story predicts

**Table 6. Predictions of the two explanations**

| Evidence | Genuine efficiency predicts | Credit outsourcing predicts | What the data show |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Credits taught per enrolled student | Flat if completers take fewer total credits; falls only if annual loads shrink | Flat: students still take full loads, but some credits are earned elsewhere | Roughly flat, 23–25 per fall undergraduate since 1998 |
| On-time vs eventual completion | Both rise | On-time rises faster, as students arrive with credits | Public: on-time +14 points, eventual +7; nonprofit +5 and +3 |
| Fewer leavers | Explains much of the rise | Explains little | 0.013–0.031 ER points in each sector: 6–14% of the public rise |
| Institutions with ER above 1 | Rare: efficiency cannot keep an institution above 1 | Common where imports are heavy | Public 4-year share tripled, to 30% |
| Where teaching per degree fell | Wherever reform took hold | Public universities fed by state pipelines, and community colleges | Public 4-year −25%, public 2-year −51%, nonprofit −8% |
| Who rises most | Institutions with the most reform | Public institutions fed by state transfer and dual-enrollment pipelines | Public R1s to 1.0; private R1s flat |
| Transfer entrants' share of degrees | No change needed | Rising, if the channel is more transfer students | Flat at about 42%: consistent with more credit per student |

### 7.2 The fundamentals, measured directly

I regress each institution's ratio on its completion rates (within four and six years for four-year institutions; within 100% and 150% of normal time for two-year), first-year retention and entering-class growth, for 2008–2024. Completion for each year comes from the graduation-rate cohort that would be graduating that year. The four-year sample has 29,538 institution-years at 2,273 institutions; the two-year sample has 17,231 at 1,662. Appendix Tables B1–B3 report the full results. Across institutions, higher six-year completion goes with a higher ratio, about 0.04 per 10 points of completion. Within institutions over time, it is faster on-time completion that matters. Retention adds little once completion is included.

Figure 13 holds all three fundamentals at their 2008 levels and recomputes the aggregate ratio. Two specifications bracket the answer: pooled regressions, which use differences across institutions, and institution fixed effects, which use changes within them.

![Figure 13](figures/WP3_13_regression_adjusted.png)

**Figure 13. Measured ER and ER with completion, retention and growth held at 2008 levels.** Regression sample only, so levels differ slightly from Figure 1. Repository tables T6b and T6c.

**Table 7. Share of the ER change explained by completion, retention and growth**

| Sample and period | Change in measured ER | Pooled OLS | Institution FE | Without completion (pooled / FE) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4-year, 2008–2022 | +0.141 | 30% | 39% | 16% / 15% |
| 4-year, 2022–2024 | −0.042 | 18% | 18% | 4% / 21% |
| Public 4-year, 2008–2022 | +0.172 | 35% | 70% | 11% / 10% |
| 2-year, 2009–2022 | +0.205 | 14% | 25% | 10% / 12% |

*Source: author's calculations from IPEDS Graduation Rates, Fall Enrollment and completions. Repository tables T6c and T14a.*

The fundamentals explain a third or so of the four-year rise, and up to 70% of the public four-year rise in the fixed-effects version. That larger number deserves two cautions. First, it is an upper bound: without year effects, a steadily trending variable like on-time completion absorbs any trending cause, and once year effects are added its within-institution coefficient collapses (from 0.54 to −0.10 at public four-year institutions). Second, and more fundamentally, completion is itself a channel for imported credit. A student who arrives with 30 dual-enrollment or AP credits finishes in four years. "Explained by completion" therefore does not mean "not outsourcing." These regressions estimate their own growth coefficients alongside completion; the timing adjustments elsewhere in the paper use the elasticities of Table 3.

### 7.3 Finishing faster, not more often

Figure 14 shows why completion needs care as an explanation, and where it changed. At public four-year institutions the share of first-time, full-time entrants who finish a bachelor's within four years rose from 31% to 45% between 2010 and 2022, while the share finishing within six years rose much less, from 56% to 63%. At private nonprofits both moved little: from 51% to 56% on time and from 64% to 67% eventually. A gain that keeps more students from leaving, such as better advising for those at risk, should raise both rates. Three things mainly raise the first: imported credit, since students who arrive with a semester or a year already completed finish sooner but not necessarily more often; fewer excess credits among students who would have finished anyway; and heavier annual loads, the aim of "15 to Finish." Section 7.4 shows that credits taught per fall student did not rise, which argues against the third. That is the pattern in the data, it accelerated after 2016, and it is far stronger at public universities.

![Figure 14](figures/WP3_14_completion.png)

**Figure 14. Four-year and six-year bachelor's completion and leavers per completer, public and private nonprofit 4-year institutions.** Cohort-weighted rates for first-time full-time entrants, by year the six-year window closes. Repository table T26.

The right-hand scale in Figure 14 tracks leavers: entrants who neither finished within six years nor were reported as transferring out, per completer. It fell at both: from 0.58 to 0.36 at public institutions and from 0.47 to 0.32 at nonprofits. Fewer leavers means fewer credits taught to students who never earn a degree there. At 15–35 credits per leaver, the fall raises the 2022 ratio by 0.013–0.031 in both sectors, which is 6–14% of the public rise and 17–41% of the nonprofit rise. The effect is about the same size in each sector, so it explains none of the gap between them: the public rise exceeded the nonprofit rise by 0.143 ER points. These rates cover first-time full-time students only, and transfer-out reporting is incomplete, so some leavers are unreported transfers. Section 8 uses the Clearinghouse's national leaver series, which follows students across institutions.

### 7.4 Teaching per student versus teaching per degree

A second test compares teaching per enrolled student with teaching per degree. Nationally, credits taught per fall undergraduate were 24.3 in 1998 and 23.7 in 2024, moving only with the business cycle, when students take heavier loads in recessions. Credits taught per degree were flat at about 175 through 2010, then fell 29% to 125 in 2022, before edging back to 133 in 2024. All of the ratio's movement is on the degree side.

Figure 15 shows where. Teaching per student stayed within a few percent of its 1998 level at public and nonprofit four-year institutions and drifted down 7–11% at public two-year colleges. Teaching per degree did not. At public two-year colleges it halved between 2010 and 2022, from 267 to 132 credits per degree. At public four-year institutions it fell by a quarter, from 160 to 120. At private nonprofits it fell 8%, from 139 to 128. Of the 52-credit national decline, public two-year colleges account for 24 credits and public four-year institutions for 21; the shift of degrees between sectors accounts for none. The large decline in teaching per degree is a public-sector phenomenon, at both levels.

![Figure 15](figures/WP3_15_credits_per_student_degree.png)

**Figure 15. Credits taught per student and per degree, by sector.** Index, 1998 = 100. Repository tables T27 and T27a.

Flat teaching per student is what outsourcing predicts: students still carry full loads, but part of their degree credit comes from elsewhere. It is also consistent with less waste, if graduates finish with fewer total credits rather than lighter loads each year. What it rules out is efficiency in the form of lighter annual loads. That the decline is concentrated at public universities and the community colleges that feed them, while nonprofit universities barely moved, fits the transfer and dual-enrollment pipelines better than a nationwide change in how students take courses.

### 7.5 Who earns the degrees

If outsourcing grew through more transfer students, the share of bachelor's degrees going to transfer entrants should have risen. It did not. The federal Outcome Measures survey follows every entering student for eight years, separately for first-time students and for those who transferred in. At public four-year institutions, 42–44% of bachelor's degrees earned within eight years go to students who transferred in, and that share is flat across all eight entering cohorts the survey covers with degree-level detail, from 2009–10 to 2016–17 (repository table T12a). A longer series is not available: each annual release reports a single entering cohort, at four, six and eight years after entry, so a six-year window would add no cohorts, and the two earlier releases (cohorts entering in 2007 and 2008) do not separate bachelor's degrees from other awards.

That share may look larger than the transfer figures the National Student Clearinghouse publishes. About 1.2 million students transferred in fall 2024, roughly 13% of non-freshman undergraduates, and only 9.4% of students who first entered college in 2019 had graduated from a different institution within six years. But those are flows measured per enrolled student or per entering cohort, not shares of degrees. Per entrant, the two sources agree. In fall 2024 about 471,000 students transferred into public four-year institutions, against 875,000 first-time freshmen: transfers are about 35% of new entrants, the same order as the 42% of degrees. The Clearinghouse data also confirm that transfer volume is not what grew. Transfers from two-year colleges into public four-year institutions fell 7% between fall 2020 and fall 2024, and the share of entering students who graduated from a different institution fell from 11.4% for the 2008 cohort to 9.4% for the 2019 cohort.

If outsourcing grew, then, it grew through more credit per graduate: transfer students arriving with more credits, and first-time students arriving with AP and dual-enrollment credit. Outcome Measures counts a student with 30 dual-enrollment credits as a first-time student.

### 7.6 Does outsourcing change what a degree means?

Hollis Robbins ([2025](https://hollisrobbinsanecdotal.substack.com/p/ai-aced-your-states-gen-ed-now-what), [2026](https://hollisrobbinsanecdotal.substack.com/p/why-sameness-not-teaching-is-the)) has argued that a university's value rests on the rigor of its courses and the capabilities of its graduates, and that when it accepts credit from elsewhere, voluntarily or by legislative mandate, it hands control of that quality to another institution. There is an irony here. Legislators demand more accountability from universities for on-time graduation and for graduates who are ready to work, while transfer mandates limit the universities' control over the foundational courses on which the rest of the curriculum builds.

At my own university, students increasingly arrive with a quarter to half of their degree credits complete, including those foundational courses. That is an observation, not a measurement, but it is the pattern the institutional data point to. If those credits prepared them poorly, the upper division is badly placed to remediate in the few semesters that remain, and the rush to finish can crowd out experiences that build professional skills. Employers rarely inspect where a graduate's credits were earned. The signal attaches to the institution whose name is on the diploma, even when that diploma rests on 60 credits of AP and community-college work and 60 credits of finishing work packed into four semesters.

Whether imported credit is actually weaker is an open question. Studies going back to Hills (1965) find "transfer shock," a drop in grades in transfer students' first term or year after transfer, which a review by Diaz (1992) put at typically half a grade point or less, with most students recovering. But they are mostly single-institution comparisons of means that do nothing about selection. The test one would want has not been run: randomly assign entering students to take Calculus I at the university or at a community college, then compare their performance in Calculus II. Short of that, universities could use their own transcripts to compare students who imported foundational courses with those who took them on campus. Nor is it obvious that the university's own version is better. Large introductory courses at research universities are often taught by graduate assistants or heavily loaded lecturers in large halls; an experienced community-college instructor may teach the same course as well or better, even if expectations differ.

## 8. Accounting for the rise

This section puts ballpark sizes on the channels that can raise the ratio, using what the earlier sections measured. It is weaker evidence than Sections 6 and 7: each row rests on an assumption, and the residual collects everything the rows miss. I do the accounting two ways (Figure 16, Table 8). The system view pools all two- and four-year institutions, nationally and then state by state; there, credit that moves between colleges nets out (Section 3.4), so the residual is mostly fewer excess credits. The four-year view covers public and private nonprofit universities only; there, credit imported from community colleges and dual enrollment does not net out and sits in the residual alongside fewer excess credits.

The two views answer different questions: the system view asks what the nation gained, the four-year view how much of the universities' gain the measured channels explain. Their difference is informative but is not a clean measure of outsourcing (Section 8.2).

![Figure 16](figures/WP3_16_accounting.png)

**Figure 16. Contributions to the 2010–2022 rise in the ER, two views.** Ranges under stated assumptions. Repository table T28.

**Table 8. Accounting for the 2010–2022 rise, two views (ER points; share of the rise)**

| Channel | How it is bounded | System: all 2- and 4-year (rise 0.236) | Public + nonprofit 4-year (rise 0.179) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cohort timing | Elasticities of Table 3 applied to each sector's entering-class growth; system view adds public 2-year colleges at −0.076 for the upper value | 0.008–0.011 (3–5%) | 0.011 (6%) |
| Fewer students leaving without a credential | 15–35 credits per leaver. System: Clearinghouse leavers per completer, 0.59 to 0.49. 4-year: IPEDS first-time full-time leavers per completer (Section 7.3) | 0.010–0.022 (4–9%) | 0.013–0.031 (7–17%) |
| AP credit (upper bound) | Qualifying exams over the prior four years × 3–6 credits, all assumed to replace college teaching | 0.012–0.024 (5–10%) | 0.016–0.030 (9–17%) |
| Associate degrees counted twice (upper bound) | Rise in the full ER minus the rise in a bachelor's-only ER | 0–0.046 (0–19%) | 0–0.022 (0–12%) |
| Residual | System: fewer excess credits by completers, other untaught credit, measurement. 4-year: the same at universities, plus credit imported from community colleges and dual enrollment | 0.134–0.207 (57–87%) | 0.085–0.139 (48–78%) |

*Source: author's calculations from IPEDS; College Board AP score distributions; National Student Clearinghouse, Yearly Progress and Completion. Repository table T28 (script 25). Components are not strictly additive. The AP row in the 4-year view assigns every qualifying exam to these institutions.*

### 8.1 The system view

Cohort timing, at the elasticities estimated in Section 4.5, accounts for 3–5% of the national rise. The attrition row uses Clearinghouse cohort outcomes: six-year completion rose six points between the 2008–10 and 2016–19 cohorts, but most of that came from fewer students still enrolled at year six, which is timing rather than avoided waste. The share who left without a credential fell only from 32.5% to 30.1%. At 15–35 credits per leaver, an assumption I cannot check, that removes 4–9% of the rise. The AP row treats every exam scoring 3 or higher as credit that replaces college teaching, which overstates its effect, and still finds at most a tenth of the rise. The associate-degree row recomputes the ratio counting only bachelor's degrees; it still rose from 0.45 to 0.64, so associate degrees, including those later followed by a bachelor's, can account for at most a fifth. Dual-enrollment credit has no row of its own: if colleges report it, it is taught inside the system and nets out like transfer credit (Section 8.3 tests that).

That leaves a residual of about 0.17 ER points at the midpoints, roughly 70% of the rise. The leading candidate is that students who finish now take fewer excess credits: fewer failed, repeated, withdrawn and abandoned courses. The halving of teaching per degree at community colleges (Section 7.4) points the same way. Some of that is plausibly genuine efficiency, the target of guided pathways, "15 to Finish" and excess-hour policies. Some of it may be easier grading. No national series on course failure and withdrawal ("DFW") rates exists, but the grade-inflation literature is suggestive. Rojstaczer and Healy document A's rising to about 43% of grades at more than 200 four-year colleges by 2008, though with D and F grades roughly stable at four-year colleges in recent years ([THE](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/node/542370)). Denning, Eide, Mumford, Patterson and Warnick (2022) find that rising grades explain most of the increase in college completion since the 1990s: first-year GPA rose 0.21 points between the high-school classes of 1992 and 2004, 11% more students cleared a 2.0, and at one college students with the same score on the same final exam received grades 0.053 points higher with each passing year ([AEJ: Applied](https://www.aeaweb.org/doi/10.1257/app.20200525)). Students who clear GPA thresholds stay enrolled and repeat fewer courses, which lowers credits taught per degree without any change in what they learned.

### 8.2 The four-year view

Restricted to public and nonprofit universities, the ratio rose 0.179. Timing explains 6%, fewer leavers 7–17%, and AP at most 9–17%, even when every qualifying exam is assigned to these institutions. Associate degrees awarded by four-year institutions add at most 12%. The residual is 0.085–0.139 ER points, nearly two-thirds of the rise at the midpoint.

This residual is an upper bound on how much of the four-year rise came from credit imported from inside the system, through transfer and dual enrollment. It is only a bound, because it also contains whatever fewer excess credits universities' own students took. The two views cannot be subtracted to isolate outsourcing: the four-year residual is not larger than the system residual, in either ER points or shares, because the system view's residual also carries the community colleges' own gains. What the four-year view does establish is that the measured, non-outsourcing channels (timing, attrition, AP and associate degrees) leave most of the public and nonprofit rise unexplained, and Section 7 showed that the fall in teaching per degree is concentrated at public universities, where it fell by a quarter while students' annual loads did not change.

### 8.3 Testing the accounting across states

The system accounting rests on assumptions the national series cannot check on its own. States offer a test. Relatively few credits cross state lines on net, so each state's system, all of its public and private two- and four-year institutions pooled, works like a small nation. States differ widely in the channels. Between 2010 and 2022, entering-class growth fell by 0.16 log points in the median state but by 0.81 in Alaska, and rose in New Hampshire. Leavers per completer fell by 0.08 in the median state. Qualifying AP exams per 100 credits taught rose from 0.30 to 0.66 in the average state, by 0.08 in Idaho and by 0.85 in Illinois. And state ratios rose by anywhere from 0.04 (the District of Columbia) to 0.33 (California).

I repeat the system accounting for each of the 51 systems, using the national parameters and state data for each input: entering-class growth by sector from IPEDS, six-year outcomes by state of the starting institution from the Clearinghouse, and the College Board's counts of qualifying AP exams from public high schools in each state. Large online institutions that enroll students nationwide, such as Western Governors, Southern New Hampshire and Phoenix, are excluded, as the Clearinghouse reports them separately from its state tables. Table 9 summarizes the results.

**Table 9. Accounting for the rise in state efficiency ratios, 2010–2022 (system view)**

| Channel | Contribution (ER points) | Share of rise | Median state's share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cohort timing (Table 3 elasticities; upper value adds public 2-year) | 0.009–0.012 | 4–5% | 3–4% |
| Fewer students leaving without a credential | 0.008–0.019 | 4–8% | 3–8% |
| AP credit (upper bound) | 0.013–0.024 | 6–11% | 5–9% |
| Associate degrees counted twice (upper bound) | 0–0.051 | 0–22% | 0–13% |
| Residual | 0.122–0.198 | 53–87% | 61–87% |

*Source: author's calculations from IPEDS; National Student Clearinghouse, Yearly Progress and Completion, State Table 2; College Board, AP Performance 2014–2024 (public schools). 51 state systems weighted by credits taught; the weighted average rise is 0.228. Repository tables T28a and T28b (script 25), building on T22.*

On average the states reproduce the national split. The value of the exercise is in the variation, which lets each assumption be checked against the data.

**Timing.** If the timing adjustment were the right size, what remains after it should be unrelated to how much each state's entering classes shrank. At the institution-level elasticities it is not: the central residual is larger in states whose entering classes shrank most (slope −0.09, standard error 0.02, credit-weighted; −0.08, standard error 0.03, unweighted). A direct regression of each state's change in the ratio on its change in entering-class growth gives −0.24 (standard error 0.04). Taken at face value, the cross-state comparison says that timing explains more of the rise in aggregate than the institution-level estimates imply, perhaps two to three times as much. But it compares states whose enrollment swings coincided with other changes, most obviously California, which had both one of the largest drops in entering classes and the Associate Degree for Transfer. I keep the institution-level elasticities and read the timing rows of Tables 8 and 9 as lower bounds.

**Leavers.** In levels, leavers matter a great deal. States with more leavers per completer teach many more credits per degree: a difference of 0.1 in leavers per completer goes with 0.03–0.07 more credits taught per degree credit, which would imply 35–75 credits per leaver, though that comparison is confounded by how much of each state's system is community colleges. In changes, the relation disappears. States where leavers per completer fell most did not see larger gains in the ratio (coefficient 0.00, standard error 0.11), and in a state-by-year panel with year effects the slope is zero. The state data cannot reject the 15–35 credits per leaver assumed nationally, but they give no sign that fewer leavers were a large part of the rise.

**AP.** States where qualifying AP exams grew more saw somewhat larger gains in the ratio. The coefficient implies 4–9 credits per qualifying exam, depending on weighting, in line with the 3–6 assumed, but its standard error is as large as the estimate. The estimate is biased toward zero, because AP is counted in the student's high-school state and many students carry it to college elsewhere; New Jersey and Illinois, the two states with the largest increases, are also large exporters of college students. AP does not explain the residual: across states the two are uncorrelated.

**Dual enrollment.** How dual enrollment enters the accounting depends on whether colleges report it. IPEDS asks institutions to include high-school students' courses in the credit hours they report. If they do, a dual-enrollment credit is taught inside the state's system and later counted inside a degree, exactly like a transfer credit. It cannot raise the state or national ratio, and the dual-enrollment credits that never become part of any degree lower it. If instead colleges leave dual-enrollment credit out of what they report, it behaves like AP: degree credit with no recorded teaching behind it, which raises the ratio.

The two years with a direct count of high-school students allow a check. Across public two-year colleges, which teach half of all dual enrollees, reported credit hours rise by about 7 for each high-school student (standard error 0.6–0.8), against 14 for each other undergraduate. Seven is about what a student taking two or three college courses a year would earn. And credits per student barely change with the dual-enrollment share: 13.1 per student enrolled during the year at colleges where high-school students are under a tenth of enrollment, and 11.0 at colleges where they are more than half. At community colleges, at least in recent years, dual-enrollment credit appears to be counted. Two gaps remain. Courses taught in high schools by high-school teachers under a college's name may be reported less completely, and no direct count exists before 2022–23 to check earlier years.

The stakes are bounded. Full-year dual enrollment grew by roughly 1.1–1.3 million students between 2010 and 2022. At 6–9 credits each, that is 7–12 million credits, 2–3% of the credits taught in 2022. If none of it were reported, it would account for 0.015–0.025 of the national rise, 6–11%. If all of it were reported and none of it counted toward a degree, it would have held the ratio down by about as much. The state data cannot settle the second: the coefficient on growth in the under-18 share of enrollment is close to zero (0.10, standard error 0.34, credit-weighted), when complete non-reporting would predict about +0.3 and complete waste about −0.3.

Taken together, the states confirm the shape of the system accounting, with one amendment. Leavers, AP and dual enrollment are each small, and in the typical state roughly two-thirds or more of the gain is common to all states and unrelated to their attrition, AP or dual-enrollment trends. Timing is the exception: the cross-state evidence suggests it matters more than the institution-level elasticities allow, so the residual is likely somewhat smaller than the central figures. What remains is what a nationwide change in how completers move through their degrees would produce: fewer failed, repeated and abandoned courses, whether through reform or easier grading.

## 9. Conclusions and implications

American colleges award far more degree credit per credit they teach than they did fifteen years ago. The national efficiency ratio sat near 0.58 from 1998 to 2011 and rose to 0.80 by 2022, before easing to 0.75. The rise was concentrated in public institutions, shared by typical rather than exceptional institutions, and present in every state. Shrinking entering classes explain little of it: at elasticities estimated within Carnegie classes, 5% of the public four-year rise and 8% of the nonprofit rise, though cross-state comparisons suggest perhaps two to three times as much.

Two interpretations compete, and the evidence divides them by level. For individual institutions, and especially public universities, the pattern as a whole fits credit outsourcing better than internal efficiency. No single fact proves it. But the sectors that moved, the institutions that crossed 1, the gap between public and private research universities, the much faster rise in on-time than eventual completion at public universities, the fall in teaching per degree at public universities and community colleges but not at nonprofits, and the growth of dual enrollment, AP and transfer-oriented certificates all point the same way. Fewer leavers explain a similar small amount in both sectors and none of the gap between them. The practical meaning is that a growing share of a public bachelor's degree is produced by high schools, community colleges and the AP program, and the university that awards it directly controls a shrinking part of it.

For the nation the verdict is more favorable. Outsourcing between colleges cannot raise the system's ratio, and the channels that can be measured, cohort timing, completion, AP and double-counted associate degrees, leave 55–87% of the rise unexplained, about 70% at the midpoints. The same holds state by state, where the unexplained part is common to every state and unrelated to each state's attrition, AP or dual-enrollment trends, though somewhat related to its enrollment swings. The most plausible reading of that residual is that students who finish now take fewer excess credits. Whether that reflects better advising and clearer degree maps, or more lenient grading that keeps students above the thresholds that would otherwise send them out or back into repeated courses, the institutional data cannot say. The distinction matters: the first is a gain in what the system teaches, the second only in what it certifies.

Three implications follow. First, the price of a degree, measured at the institution that awards it, rose far less than the price of a credit: 18% against 55% in real terms since 2002 on published tuition, not at all on net tuition revenue, and less than nothing on the net cost of attendance. Part of that is a genuine saving and part is cost moved to cheaper providers, where grant aid now covers the tuition of the average first-time, full-time community-college student. Second, institution-level statistics on cost per degree, spending per degree and completion now describe a smaller piece of a student's education than they used to, and comparisons across institutions and over time should account for that. Third, a degree assembled from AP, dual-enrollment and community-college credit is a different product from one taught in full by the university that awards it. It may be as good, or better. But that is an empirical question that almost no one is in a position to answer, because the data needed to answer it sit in individual institutions' transcript files.

### Open questions

- **Why the ratio fell after 2022.** Cohort growth explains about 8% of the four-year decline; the rest may reflect degree counts falling with the small COVID-era entering classes, more credits taught to returning and part-time students, or provisional 2024 data.
- **How big the timing effect is.** Institution-level elasticities (Table 3) and cross-state comparisons (Section 8.3) disagree by a factor of two to three. A two-year elasticity has not been estimated.
- **Policy effects.** The adoption years in Table 1, completed for all states, would allow the state public-system ratio to serve as an outcome around adoption dates.
- **Transcripts.** The High School Longitudinal Study of 2009, linked to postsecondary transcripts, measures dual-enrollment and AP credit at entry and total credits at degree for a national cohort, and could test the institutional patterns directly.
- **Course failure and withdrawal.** A national series on DFW rates, from transcript studies or a state system's course-level records, would show how much of the residual is fewer failed and repeated courses.
- **Measurement choices.** Whether the headline should be a four-year-only ratio, which price measure to show for states (Figures 8–8c), and whether general-education certificates should be excluded from certificate-weighted measures.

## Appendix A. Data and construction

**Panel.** The panel covers U.S. 2- and 4-year institutions from 1992 to 2024; 1995 and 1997 are missing because the credit-hour item was not collected. The paper uses 1998 onward, the first unbroken annual series. All measures are institution-level and within a single academic year. 2024 data are provisional.

**Credit hours.** 12-month undergraduate credit-hour activity. From 2002 it comes from the 12-Month Enrollment survey. Before that it comes from the same item in Institutional Characteristics (1992–1994, 1996, 1998–1999) and Fall Enrollment Part D (2000–2001). Quarter-calendar credits are divided by 1.5. From 2004 the divisor comes from the full-time-equivalent formula. Before 2002 it comes from the institution's own calendar-system field; for 2004–2010 the two agree 98.1% of the time.

**Degrees.** First-major bachelor's (120 credits) and associate degrees (60). Certificates enter only the certificate-weighted variant, at duration weights of 8 (under 12 weeks), 20 (12 weeks to under a year), 18 (under a year, pre-2020 code), 45 (one to two years) and 90 (two to four years).

**Screens**, applied identically in every year:

1. 2- and 4-year institutions only.
2. At least 30 credit hours.
3. ER no higher than 3 and below the 99.5th percentile for the institution type.
4. A completions record that year.
5. Credit hours per fall undergraduate inside the national 0.5–99.5% band.
6. No year in which credit hours per student fall below 0.6 or rise above 1.67 times the institution's own median. This last screen removes unit errors, such as institutions that reported courses rather than credits before 2007.

From 2006 on, the screens move the national ratio by at most 0.009. The pre-2002 years are noisier: 2000 and 2001 lose 27% and 45% of credit hours to the screens. A stable panel of about 2,500 institutions present in at least 26 of 31 years follows the same path: 0.60 (1998), 0.59 (2002), 0.59 (2010), 0.81 (2022).

**Entering-class growth.** For four-year institutions, (Eₜ + Eₜ₋₁) ÷ (Eₜ₋₄ + Eₜ₋₅), where Eₜ is first-time degree-seeking entrants in the fall that opens year t, from Fall Enrollment back to 1986. For two-year colleges, described but not used in adjustments, (Eₜ + Eₜ₋₁) ÷ (Eₜ₋₂ + Eₜ₋₃). Sector growth sums entrants over the sector's institutions.

**Growth adjustment.** Net-of-growth ER for sector s: ERₛₜ × exp(−eₛ × (ln Gₛₜ − ln Gₛ,1998)), with e = −0.076 for public and −0.128 for private nonprofit 4-year institutions (Table 3, columns 2 and 4). Repository scripts 19 and 20, tables T23, T23b, T24.

**Completion and leavers by control.** Graduation Rates, first-time full-time bachelor's-seeking subcohort: adjusted cohort, completers within four years and within 150% of normal time, any completer within 150%, and transfer-outs. Leavers per completer = (cohort − completers − transfer-outs) ÷ completers. Year = the year the 150% window closes. Script 22, tables T26 and T26a.

**Regression variables (Section 7.2).**

- *Completion:* from the Graduation Rates release whose cohort graduates in the year. For four-year institutions, within 4 years and within 150% of normal time; for two-year institutions, within 100% and 150%.
- *Retention:* full-time first-year retention.
- *Growth:* as above.

**Accounting (Tables 8 and 9).** National degree and credit totals; College Board AP score distributions, 2004–2024; National Student Clearinghouse six-year outcomes by entering cohort (system view) and IPEDS leavers per completer by control (four-year view).

- *AP:* AP credits flowing into year t equal qualifying exams averaged over years t−4 to t−1, times 3–6 credits. The AP contribution is the actual rise minus the rise in degree credits ÷ (credits taught + AP credits).
- *Attrition:* adds back k × (change in leavers per completer) × 2022 completers to 2022 credits taught, for k = 15–35.
- *Timing:* each adjusted sector's 2022 degree credits are deflated by exp(e × change in log growth, 2010–2022).
- *States:* each state's system pools all of its in-sample 2- and 4-year institutions, excluding large multi-state online institutions. Leavers use Clearinghouse State Table 2. AP allocates the national flow of qualifying exams to states by each state's share of public-school qualifying exams. Scripts 18 and 25, tables T22–T22c and T28–T28b.

**Policy adoption years (Table 1).** Compiled from statutes, system policies and secondary sources; file `data/external/state_policy_adoption_dates_2026-10-04.md` lists each year with its source. The Education Commission of the States comparison tables could not be retrieved automatically, so coverage is partial.
